cohort: Standard full-time English language variant. The English/Dutch option changes tutorial language, with shared curriculum and plenary instruction.

courseDetails.name: Introduction to Anthropology
courseDetails.entry: Please note: readings and lectures will be in English. Students can submit written work in English or Dutch.
courseDetails.contents: The lectures and literature discussed in the tutorials provide students with a general introduction to anthropology. The lectures and the textbook offer an overview of anthropological themes, concepts and theories. The lectures also serve as an introduction to complementary assigned readings, which will be discussed in the tutorials. In these tutorials, the focus is on identifying, understanding, and critically assessing the main arguments in the assigned readings.Introduction to Anthropology is complemented by the course Current Debates 1: Connecting Worlds.

courseDetails.name: Ethnographies and Academic Writing
courseDetails.entry: Only accessible to first-year major students in Anthropology. Please note: readings and lectures will be in English. Students can submit written work in English or Dutch.
courseDetails.contents: The study material consists of a selection of monographs that speak to a number of theoretical debates and currents within anthropology. These debates and the (academic) context within which the books were written are elaborated on in the lectures and critically discussed during the tutorials.

courseDetails.name: Philosophy of Science
courseDetails.entry: Only accessible to first-year major students in anthropology. Please note: readings and lectures will be in English. Students can submit written work in English or Dutch.
courseDetails.contents: Ever since the social sciences came into being, the question has been raised whether social science could or should model itself after the natural sciences. Although many in the natural sciences as well as in the social sciences tend to highlight their mutual differences, both grapple with the same basic epistemological and ontological questions:Can we distinguish science from non-science? And if so, how?What is the nature of existence? The answer to this question defines our objects of research, leading to the question: what can we know about these objects, and how can we produce knowledge of them in the first place?How is science shaped by — and how does it shape — culture, society, and relations of power?Whose knowledge counts, and what happens to ways of knowing that fall outside dominant scientific frameworks?Apart from these general philosophy of science questions, we discuss the relation between science and society:How is science part of, and articulated by, culture and society? And knowing that science is a social product that helps to (re)produce society, how do scientists deal with this?Especially in this age of "alternative facts," how can social scientists make and defend truth claims — and what does it mean to take seriously the knowledge of communities whose expertise is routinely discounted?In this course we explore these issues through a set of seminal readings — from Popper and Kuhn through Haraway, Hacking, Mignolo, and Liboiron — and connect them to live contemporary controversies including climate denial, vaccination hesitancy, forever chemicals, and the politics of AI-generated evidence.

courseDetails.name: Current Debates 1: Connecting Worlds
courseDetails.entry: Participation in Introduction to Anthropology, Ethnographies and Academic Writing, Philosophy of Science. Please note: readings and lectures will be in English. Students can submit written work in English or Dutch.
courseDetails.contents: After being introduced to general anthropological knowledge and concepts in the complementary first-year course Introduction to Anthropology (IA), Current Debates 1: Connecting Worlds takes the knowledge that you’ve acquired during IA “on the road” by exploring the connections between global/planetary frameworks for social change and the ways in which communities navigate and influence these frameworks through local practices. This course does so through several distinct, yet interconnected themes in anthropology: the Nation-State, Economy & Development, and Globalisation, analysing them through a historical and comparative lens, to elucidate their interconnectedness in the present day.The lectures are intended to contextualise, illustrate, and expand the main themes in the literature. In smaller working groups (tutorials), students discuss the content of the lectures and literature in depth, give group presentations, and work on assignments. The course places a high demand on participation in the tutorials.You are expected to prepare yourself for each meeting by completing the assigned readings, documentaries and/or podcasts. You will only get out of the class as much as you put into it. You are advised to come to the tutorials with prepared questions, comments, and concerns.Successful completion of this course is a prerequisite for entry into its complementary second-year course, Current Debates 2: Imagining Futures.

courseDetails.name: Anthropological Research Methods
courseDetails.entry: Only accessible to first-year majors in Anthropology. Participation in Introduction to Anthropology, Ethnographies and Academic Writing, Philosophy of Science. Please note: readings and lectures will be in English. Students can submit written work in English or Dutch.
courseDetails.contents: The course consists of lectures and tutorials. The lectures offer topical introductions which students apply to their own projects. At the start of the course, students will form small groups in the tutorials, based on shared topics of interest they will conduct research on. They will work in these research teams for the entire course through a series of group assignments as well as an individual assignment. Group research projects are coached during tutorials through method-specific assignments such as research problem design, participant observation, interviews, and a survey. These also provide practical insight into possible dilemmas and problems, such as preparation and informed consent, recruitment, data collection, qualitative and basic quantitative analysis, interpretation and presentation. The course is closed with an individual examination.

courseDetails.name: Doing Anthropology
courseDetails.entry: Only accessible to first-year majors in Anthropology. Participation in Introduction to Anthropology, Ethnographies and Academic Writing, Philosophy of Science. Please note: readings and lectures will be in English. Students can submit written work in English or Dutch.
courseDetails.contents: The course presents a series of ‘talk show-format’ interviews with anthropologists working in diverse fields. This is followed by a pressure cooker practical assignment, and an exercise to stimulate self-reflection. This threefold approach is reflected in teaching methods, as well as in the built-up of the course design:In the first week, guests to our ‘Anthro talk show’ will share their experiences with doing anthropology. The second week involves a pressure cooker assignment in which students apply their anthropological skills and knowledge as well as their inventiveness and creative thinking. They formulate an applied research question on one of the suggested subjects in order to solve part of that larger puzzle. They present their piece of the puzzle in a seminar at the end of the course. Students are encouraged to be creative! They can choose to present their findings as a written essay but are also free to make a podcast, a video or a photo exhibition.In the third week, students will write a personal reflection/vision paper which focuses on their personal trajectories, future ambitions and how anthropology might fit into those.

courseDetails.name: Theory and History of Anthropology
courseDetails.entry: 42 ECTS of the first academic year in Anthropology, including Introduction to Anthropology. Please note: readings and lectures will be in English. Students can submit written work in English or Dutch.
courseDetails.contents: Theory and History of Anthropology offers students insight into the historical developments that contributed to the emergence of the dominant theoretical schools with the discipline of anthropology. Departing from Eurocentric schema that locate anthropology squarely in north western Europe and the United States, and adding updated chronologies that introduce theories from the South or by subalternized populations in the second half of the 20th century, this course presents anthropology as always already having been a global set of critical conversations among a wide variety of peoples.The first half of the course (block 1) is dedicated to classical theoretical schools in anthropology such as evolutionism, functionalism, structural-functionalism, Marxism, and symbolic anthropology. In the second bloc more recent paradigmatic traditions such postcolonialism, feminism, and Foucauldian approaches.

courseDetails.name: Current Debates 2: Imagining Futures
courseDetails.entry: 42 ECTS of the first year of Anthropology, including Current Debates 1: Connecting Worlds. Please note: readings and lectures will be in English. Students can submit written work in English or Dutch.
courseDetails.contents: Current Debates 2: Imagining Futures explores some of the world’s most pressing current issues - such as the climate catastrophe, precarity, racialization, the far right, and the impact of technological revolutions - and examines the ways anthropologists today are investigating them. Students will read three anthropological monographs. CD2 builds upon the knowledge of theory that students have already mastered in CD1 and THA, and asks them to use this basis to engage with the current ways anthropologists think about the conditions and possibilities of our world right now. It invites students to grapple with recent global developments through these theories, and then asks students to imagine futures, using the skills and knowledge they have mastered in this course. Please note that the course manual is subject to change.

courseDetails.name: Practicing Ethnography
courseDetails.entry: 42 EC of the first year of Anthropology, including: Ethnographies and Academic Writing and Anthropological Research Methods. Participation in: Theory and History of Anthropology and/or Current Debates 2: Imagining Futures and an exploration course. Please note: readings and lectures will be in English. Students can submit written work in English or Dutch.
courseDetails.contents: In this course, students will deepen their understanding of, and hone their skills in, ethnographic research. They will do so in an integrated manner, by going through the full cycle of ethnographic research: including research design, one month of fieldwork, data-analysis, and ethnographic writing – and, in the applied track, reporting back to the organization. In small groups, students will research a theme of their own choosing – or, in the applied track, investigate a question raised by an external organization. Each team will present the results in a portfolio and a presentation, while working towards an end product in which group work and individual work are combined in the form of an “edited volume,” in which each student contributes an individual essay, framed by a collectively written introduction. In the applied track, the collective part of the end product can take the form of a report with recommendations for the partner organization. Please pay attention - there are 6 tutorials. When registering for this course, you can choose from 5 options: the language in which the tutorial is given (Dutch or English) and whether the groups belong to the general or the applied track. There are three different applied groups (A, B and C), each with different projects:Nederlands/Dutch (general)Engels/English (general)Applied A (Nederlands/Dutch)Applied B (Engels/English)Applied C (Engels/English)

courseDetails.name: Body and Culture
courseDetails.entry: Majors in anthropology: 42 EC from year 1 anthropology and participation in Theory and History of Anthropology (THA) and/or Current Debates 2: Imagining Futures (CD2). If you follow Anthropological Research Methods and Current Debates 1: Connecting Worlds you can NOT register for the exploration courses. If you only follow Anthropological Research Methods, or only Current Debates 1: Connection Worlds, you are allowed to register for one exploration course (provided you have obtained 42 EC from year 1). For minor students in anthropology, the entry requirement is: Introduction to Anthropology. Please note: readings and lectures will be in English. Students can submit written work in English or Dutch.
courseDetails.contents: The anthropological study of the body knows a variety of approaches. Some researchers study how people use the body as a symbol or metaphor for society. Others emphasise the instrumental characteristics of the body. Again others use the body to study self-understanding and/or in relation to processes of normalisation. In medical anthropology the focus is more often than not on the variety of ideas about the healthy and the ill body and how different ideas translate into practices. Feminist anthropology focuses more on the social organization or inequality and processes of in- and exclusion on the basis of gender, race/ethnicity, sex, sexual identity, age, disability, et cetera. Whereas there are overlaps we will discuss the outcomes of the different approaches to the production of scholarly knowledge. The notion of embodiment will be analysed to understand the ubiquity of the body in all kinds of cultural expressions, including politics, religion, sexuality, popular culture, and there will be specific attention to the experiencing body and the question of agency.

courseDetails.name: Ecology and Economy: Green Futures
courseDetails.entry: Majors in anthropology: 42 EC from year 1 anthropology and participation in Theory and History of Anthropology (THA) and/or Current Debates 2: Imagining Futures (CD2). If you follow Anthropological Research Methods and Current Debates 1: Connecting Worlds you can NOT register for the exploration courses. If you only follow Anthropological Research Methods, or only Current Debates 1: Connection Worlds, you are allowed to register for one exploration course (provided you have obtained 42 EC from year 1). For minor students in anthropology, the entry requirement is: Introduction to Anthropology. Please note: readings and lectures will be in English. Students have to submit written work in English.
courseDetails.contents: This is a reading-intensive course divided into two parts, requiring active participation in lectures and reading groups.The first part introduces diverse capitalist projects that have transformed the relationship between ecology and economy. We begin by examining how biodiversity discourses shape the economic imagination and visual culture of bioprospecting. Then, we explore the relationship between ecology and economy under supply-chain and technoscientific capitalisms. Finally, we study market-based solutions to environmental issues and the relationship between markets and policy.The second part discusses the main critiques of capitalism in times of ecological crisis. We begin with ecosocialist and abolitionist critiques of the Anthropocene and extractivism. We also examine how degrowth has become a thriving transdisciplinary academic field concerned with the future of agriculture, corporate power, and outer space. Lastly, we explore emerging debates in environmental justice from a multispecies perspective.The lectures introduce students to scholarship by anthropologists, sociologists, economists, political theorists, and scholars in science and technology studies.

courseDetails.name: Anthropology of Contemporary South Asia
courseDetails.entry: Anthropology UvA-students: 42 ECTS. If any vacancies, students from other studies: first year completed (60 ECTS). Minor Anthropology students: Introduction to Anthropology. Anthropology UvA students are prioritized in registration for this course. Please note: readings and lectures will be in English. Students have to submit written work in English.
courseDetails.contents: Since the turn of the millenium, social and political life in South Asia has been in the threos of transitions. The course will explore how these transitions have been explored anthropologically. What theories and methods have anthropologists applied to understand cultural configurations in and of transient processes? What epistemologies has this anthropological knowledge depended on and how does that differ from frameworks of the past? How has the vast body of anthropological insights produced in relation to evolving social situations in contemporary south Asia connected to global anthropological theory? The countries of South Asia - Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka - are internally diverse, but have all experiened multiple transitions. The course will focus on anthropolgical work in the areas of:rural-urban transitions, particularly the rise of urbanism and accompanying exclusions;Markets, the liberalization of the economy, neo-liberalism and the changes wrought by this on relations among people;Science and Technology - investment in technolgies for development and their impacts on institutions;Democracy, politics and the state, partcularly transforming state-citizen relations. These areas will be divided across the weeks of the course, introducing pertinent anthropological writing in the form of monographs and journal articles.

courseDetails.name: Future Perspectives
courseDetails.entry: First academic year in Anthropology (60 EC), Theory and History of Anthropology (THA) and/or Current Debates 2: Imagining Futures (CD2) and an Exploration Course. Please note: readings and lectures will be in English. Students can submit written work in English or Dutch.
courseDetails.contents: This course combines on-site lectures, events, and group training with online exercises and assignments. It features both individual and group components, challenging students to contemplate their professional life beyond their current studies and further develop their own career interests. Participants will connect with professionals in fields aligned with these interests and reflect on their learning during their Bachelor's program, identifying areas for further development. Additionally, students will evaluate their personal networks and are challenged to expand their reach. At a concluding conference, students will showcase their analysis of future career trends and opportunities for anthropologists through a poster presentation and engage in discussions about their work during panel conversations.This course has two complementary courses: Doing Anthropology in the first year and Professional Anthropological Profile later in the third year.

courseDetails.name: Professional Anthropological Profile
courseDetails.entry: First academic year in Anthropology (60 EC), Theory and History of Anthropology (THA) and/or Current Debates 2: Imagining Futures (CD2) and an Exploration Course. Participation in: Future Perspectives (FP) Please note: readings and lectures will be in English. Students can submit written work in English or Dutch.
courseDetails.contents: This course combines on-site lectures, events, and group training with online exercises and assignments. It features mainly individual components, challenging students to apply the knowledge acquired throughout their entire Bachelor’s to critically reflect on their individual learning trajectory into becoming an anthropologist, and to further develop their particular career interests. Based on these reflections, students will design a professional anthropological profile through which they can showcase the transferable skills and personal ethics they have developed during the Bachelor’s programme to future academic and/or non-academic employers or commissioning parties. This course is the culmination of two previously taken courses: Doing Anthropology in the first year and the third-year course, Future Perspectives.

courseDetails.name: Anthropology of Health
courseDetails.entry: First academic year in Anthropology (60 EC), Theory and History of Anthropology (THA) and/or Current Debates 2: Imagining Futures (CD2), an Exploration Course and Practicing Ethnography. Please note: readings and lectures will be in English. Students have to submit written work in English.
courseDetails.contents: Drawing on ethnographic texts we will pay attention to how people ‘do’ health in everyday situations, analyzing practices like healthy eating, wellness, and self-care. The course will also get you ready to critically and carefully analyze biomedicine and public health, institutions that medical anthropologists have understood as hegemonic, although, in a post-COVID world, they often seem fragile.Theoretically the course builds on and consolidates knowledge of critical theory, bio and necropolitics, and abolitionist approaches to public health. Studying care, epistemic (in)justices in health and structural violence, the course assessment and in-class discussion challenges you to come up with ways of doing public health differently.Throughout the course students will be supported – via a series of hands-on writing workshops – to produce a well-researched and conceptualized essay on a topic of their choosing.

courseDetails.name: Presentation Anthropology of Health
courseDetails.entry: First academic year in Anthropology (60 EC), Theory and History of Anthropology and/or Current Debates 2: Imagining Futures, an Exploration Course and Practicing Ethnography. The course is only accessible to anthropology majors who are enrolled in the corresponding theme module.
courseDetails.contents: This is the Presentation Theme Course that follows the Theme Course Anthropology of Health. Only accessible to anthropology majors. Please note that you need to register for the presentation theme course that matches the corresponding theme course you are taking.

courseDetails.name: Anthropology of Dance: Religion, Ritual and the Body
courseDetails.entry: First academic year in Anthropology (60 EC), Theory and History of Anthropology (THA) and/or Current Debates 2: Imagining Futures (CD2), an exploration course and Practicing Ethnography. Please note: readings and lectures will be in English. Students have to submit written work in English.

courseDetails.entry: First academic year in Anthropology (60 EC), Theory and History of Anthropology and/or Current Debates 2: Imagining Futures, an Exploration Course and Practicing Ethnography. The course is only accessible to anthropology majors who are enrolled in the corresponding theme module.
courseDetails.contents: This is the Presentation Theme Course that follows the Theme Course Anthropology of Dance: Religion, Ritual and the Body. Please note that you need to register for the presentation theme course that matches the corresponding theme course you are taking.

choiceProof: The published choice spaces are retained. A feasible example takes Anthropology of Contemporary South Asia in block 1, Body and Culture and Ecology and Economy in block 4, and the open 6 EC in the second semester. Year three uses Anthropology of Health and its block 2 presentation in semester 1, and Anthropology of Dance and its block 5 presentation in semester 2. Each semester has 18 EC of taught work and 12 EC of electives in year three.
progression: The three fall foundations precede methods, Connecting Worlds and Doing Anthropology. Passing year one provides 60 EC, including Introduction and Connecting Worlds, satisfying the 42 EC binding study advice and course-entry thresholds for the year-two sequence.

The Exploration restriction applies to concurrent registration in first-year Methods and Connecting Worlds. In the standard adopted sequence those registrations end in year one. Theory and Current Debates 2 are followed before the block 4 Exploration courses. Completed first-year ethnographic writing and methods, followed by second-year theory, debates and Exploration, satisfy Practicing Ethnography.

The regular pathway completes Practicing Ethnography and Exploration before either theme course or its linked presentation. Future Perspectives precedes Professional Anthropological Profile. The 12 EC year-two project contains one month of fieldwork, group research and individually written work. The regular programme uses paired theme courses and presentations in year three and has no separately credited final-year thesis.
